label: pr:unit
title: Design principle
body_md:
\label{pr:unit}
A fraction is introduced as the result of sharing one unit fairly: the unit is cut into $b$ equal parts and $a$ of them are taken. The unit is one continuous object, never a collection. This definition belongs to the world of sharing; Principle~\ref{pr:linear} is intended to establish its numerical interpretation through measure, and from Grade~6 the quotient characterisation ($\frac{a}{b}$ is the number which, multiplied by $b$, gives $a$) becomes the operative definition.
head: environment
name: A fair share of one unit

title: Terminology
body_md: The distinction between \emph{unit} and \emph{whole} is a convention of this design, not a general restriction on mathematical usage. In the world of sharing, \emph{unit} names the continuous reference object whose equal parts are considered; \emph{whole} is used for a collection or quantity such as twelve beads. In the world of measure, a reference length $U$ is assigned measure~$1$, and a length $L$ has numerical measure $r$ when $L=rU$. The number~$1$, the reference length and its physical or graphic representation are distinct. A paper strip has a physical length even when no value in centimetres is specified. In early tasks the reference is kept stable, and ``a length of $\frac{2}{3}$'' abbreviates a length measuring $\frac{2}{3}$ in that reference unit. Changing the reference is mathematically legitimate; the reasons for postponing it are didactic (Section~\ref{sec:crossing}).
head: manual

label: def:fraction
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:fraction}
A fraction has two numbers separated by a fraction bar. The \emph{denominator}, below the bar, tells how many equal parts the unit is divided into; the \emph{numerator}, above the bar, tells how many of those parts are taken.
head: environment
name: Fraction, Grade 1, in substance

label: pr:linear
title: Design principle
body_md:
\label{pr:linear}
The share is represented by a bar cut into equal parts: an object that is at once a shared unit and a length. The bar is intended to support a transition from sharing to measure. In Grade~3, rulers graduated in fractions of a specified unit and points on the number line explicitly represent the fraction as a number. This describes the teaching intention, not evidence that the transition has occurred for each pupil. Other representations are used for specific purposes and related back to the bar.
head: environment
name: The bar as a bridge, the number line as arrival

label: pr:ratio
title: Design principle
body_md:
\label{pr:ratio}
A fraction is first taught as a number. The progression postpones the explicit conceptualisation and the symbolic treatment of the fraction as a scalar operator---the scaling $x\mapsto\frac{a}{b}\,x$, written $\frac{a}{b}\times N$---not the application of fractions to quantities, which fair sharing provides from Grade~1. ``Two thirds of thirty'' is treated as a situation, a part--whole relation on a quantity in which the number $\frac{2}{3}$ is applied. Such situations, and part--part ratios written $a:b$, are developed in a companion \emph{ratio} strand, where they receive their meaning from fair sharing; the fraction strand prioritises numerical meaning and schedules explicit operator notation after work on magnitude, equivalence and arithmetic. This order is intended to consolidate numerical meaning; the schedule alone does not establish that pupils have achieved it. The order is one of institutionalisation, not of encounter: a meaning may be met, or used locally, in either strand before it is stated (Section~\ref{sec:encounter}).
head: environment
name: Numbers before explicit operators

label: pr:technique
title: Design principle
body_md:
\label{pr:technique}
A result needed before its full theoretical status is accessible should receive an informal explanation in the model and a mathematically valid local justification using available knowledge; its formal generalisation may be deferred. Validity conditions must be respected from the first use and made explicit in language appropriate to the task. An activity can embody a condition before pupils formulate it verbally. The audit distinguishes this implicit constraint from an explicit statement and identifies where a local justification is still a proposed revision.
head: environment
name: Technique before formalism

label: pr:chain
title: Design principle
body_md:
\label{pr:chain}
The intended convention for a multi-step calculation is a chain of equal expressions, with one transformation per step. Chains appear in Grades~2--3; written reasons are introduced in lessons from Grade~4 and occur unevenly in model answers. The vertical layout is intended to support later algebraic work, while equality of expressions and equivalence of equations require separate teaching.
head: environment
name: The chain of equalities

label: h:magnitude
title: Hypothesis
body_md:
\label{h:magnitude}
Explicit coordination of a shared bar, its measured length and a point on the number line improves transfer between representations by Grade~5, beyond practice with the representations separately. Measures include unpartitioned number-line estimation on $[0,1]$ and $[0,2]$, and comparisons with different numerators and denominators. Transfer items ask pupils to recognise or produce the same fraction across a partitioned bar, a length relative to a supplied unit and an unpartitioned line, without prescribing a conversion procedure. Diagram size, orientation and the extent of the drawn line vary while the reference is specified. A combined share--measure--place item assesses coordination with support; separate, unfamiliar items assess less-cued transfer. Code identification of the unit, agreement of numerical values, explanations and whole-number-bias errors separately, so consistent but incorrect responses do not count as successful transfer.
head: environment

label: h:units
title: Hypothesis
body_md:
\label{h:units}
Keeping the reference stable in the initial fraction tasks supports numerical meaning without a practically important later disadvantage in coordinating units. In Grades~3--5, measures include locating fractions on lines extending beyond~$1$, measuring bars longer than the designated strip and recognising the same fraction in proportionally resized diagrams. At the end of Grade~6, use two distinct probes: (i) two strips, $20$~cm and $10$~cm, each designated as one unit, whose halves have equal numerical measures in their respective units but different physical lengths; (ii) one unchanged $6$~cm segment measured with reference strips of $8$~cm and $4$~cm, giving $\frac{3}{4}$ and $\frac{3}{2}$. Record whether pupils preserve the specified reference and distinguish number from physical length. The second probe tests reunitisation directly; operator success is not its substitute. Compare with a curriculum introducing unit changes earlier, record any explicit teaching of reunitisation in either group, and distinguish unprompted transfer from performance after such instruction. Non-inferiority is a testable prediction, not a conclusion licensed by the present design analysis.
head: environment

label: h:operator
title: Hypothesis
body_md:
\label{h:operator}
Prior work establishing fraction magnitude, followed by explicit treatment of scalar multiplication, improves pupils' ability to use $\frac{2}{3}$ as a number without an immediate part--whole context, while preserving performance on applications to quantities. At the end of Grade~6, assess context-free placement and comparison alongside ``$\frac{2}{3}$ of $30$'', with matched comparison groups. Ask what $\frac{2}{3}$ means and allow words or drawings. Code action descriptions, perceptual part--whole descriptions, measures relative to a unit and numerical relations as distinct response categories; they are not assumed to form a validated developmental scale. Interpret them with performance and explanations across several items, rather than treating one preferred wording as evidence of understanding. Record the actual timing of explicit operator instruction in both strands.
head: environment

label: h:improper
title: Hypothesis
body_md:
\label{h:improper}
Pupils who meet unit-fraction iteration in the Grade~2 material (``three eighths is three times one eighth'') place fractions greater than one more accurately when they reach the Grade~4 material than pupils taught the counting reading alone. Measure: placing $\frac{5}{3}$ and $\frac{7}{4}$ on lines from $0$ to $2$ that are either unpartitioned or partitioned in a non-matching way (sixths, eighths), so that counting the target numerator's number of given intervals does not suffice; code refusals, placements below~$1$ and use of the whole line as the unit \citep{bright1988}. Ask pupils to identify the unit fraction they iterated. Correct placement remains an indicator rather than proof of an iterative scheme, since learned conversions can also succeed.
head: environment

label: h:ratio
title: Hypothesis
body_md:
\label{h:ratio}
The explicit part--part/part--whole distinction of the ratio strand (Principle~\ref{pr:ratio}) reduces the reading of a part--part ratio $a:b$ as ``$\frac{a}{b}$ of the total''. Measure: problems giving a part--part ratio and asking for the fraction of the whole, at the end of Grade~6.
head: environment

label: h:chain
title: Hypothesis
body_md:
\label{h:chain}
Documented practice in explaining successive fraction transformations from the primary levels reduces invalid transformations and improves error detection in later algebraic simplifications. Compare with instruction matched for mathematical content and opportunities to explain reasoning, while varying the use of written equality chains. Assess unfamiliar expressions, valid and invalid transformations, and reasons for accepting or rejecting them. Record use of the taught layout separately as compliance with a convention. The current corpus's uneven annotations mean that this hypothesis concerns the intended practice; exposure must be checked in an empirical study.
head: environment

label: h:domain
title: Hypothesis
body_md:
\label{h:domain}
Explicitly retaining the original domain beside algebraic cancellations reduces domain loss after simplification in Grade~8. Items ask for the original domain, a simplified expression on that domain and whether both expressions have the same natural domain. Correctly inheriting a condition from the question is distinguished from asserting an unrestricted identity.
head: environment

label: h:cancel
title: Hypothesis
body_md:
\label{h:cancel}
The explicit contrast between $\frac{x+2}{2}$ (not identically $x$) and $\frac{2x+4}{2}$ in Grade~8 reduces the cancellation of terms of a sum. Measure: simplification items mixing sums and products in numerator and denominator.
head: environment
